paths.title: Checking the computation
paths.question: How can someone check an answer?
paths.description: Cryptographic proofs let a computer show that it followed a particular calculation. These notes cover the verifier and the cost of proving encrypted work.

paths.title: Learning while encrypted
paths.question: Can the model keep changing?
paths.description: Follow new examples into an encrypted model, then see how it answers questions and replaces old memories.

paths.title: Private AI
paths.question: Who can read the model’s memory?
paths.description: We want an AI to learn and communicate without giving its host unrestricted access to its internal state.

steps.label: The system we want to build
A design that exposed too much

cards.title: A learner that keeps learning
cards.body: The latest prototype sorts software issues into categories. You can teach it new examples, ask questions, and restart it without losing its memory. Each category keeps its eight most recent examples. A complete nine-category run included 18 teachings, three questions and two old examples being replaced; the encrypted scores matched the ordinary calculation throughout.

cards.title: Faster proofs for encrypted learning
cards.metric_label: for 12 teachings, four questions and a restart
cards.body: Encryption and proof systems often use different arithmetic, which makes checking the work expensive. We built a proof system using the same arithmetic as the encryption. It completes a two-category learning session with 3,200 proofs checked. Verification is still slower than simply repeating this small encrypted computation.

cards.title: Checking every step of an encrypted calculation
cards.body: We repaired a bug that left the final row of a calculation unchecked. The corrected version proves a complete encrypted similarity calculation, including multiplication and rescaling. A more compact way to check number ranges reduces proof size by 8.19%; total proving time improves by 1.69%, with higher memory use.

cards.title: The first text-to-encrypted-answer demo
cards.body: An earlier prototype connected new text examples to encrypted model updates and answers. Two teachings and two category answers completed in 21.20 seconds. Later work found a missing final-row check in its proof generator; the corrected implementation is used by the current learner.

cards.title: Adding memories can also expose them
cards.body: One proposed design gave the software a key for adding new memories. Our calculation showed that combining that key with the answer keys would reveal all 576 changing coordinates of the model. That design needs a different way to add memories before it can protect them from its host.

cards.title: Connecting the proof verifier to its mathematics
cards.body: A verifier checks a large computation by sampling parts of a mathematical encoding. We connected its batching and folding calculations to a Lean theorem about the probability of accepting an invalid proof. The theorem assumes fresh independent randomness; connecting that assumption to the implemented hash-based transcript is further work.

cards.title: A design for passing private state to the next step
cards.body: We developed a theoretical design in which each step certifies the next private state and the answer it may release. It can track that ancestry without an online registry. It depends on program obfuscation, erased setup secrets and a preset number of steps. An efficient implementation is still missing.

cards.title: Encrypted answers match ordinary arithmetic
cards.body: A small model processed 384 updates and replaced 256 old examples while encrypted. All 96 numerical answers matched the ordinary calculation, and 28 of 32 final category predictions were correct. The encrypted run took about 3 minutes 40 seconds.

cards.title: Better text features for a small learner
cards.body: A small learner used features from the SmolLM3 language model to adapt to recent examples. It reached 91.1% accuracy, compared with 51.0% using the original features. These tests used synthetic texts and histories. The language model that produced the features ran outside encryption.

cards.title: Giving different readers different answers
cards.body: A functional-encryption prototype gives each recipient keys for a fixed set of questions. It completed 384 updates and 96 queries, with all numerical answers matching the reference. Those keys still work on old inputs and outside the application, so deleting an example from the model does not revoke access to it.

cards.title: Setting up without a central master secret
cards.body: This prototype creates the public setup without generating a central secret key. It completed 40 updates, four queries and eight replacements, and reopened the same saved history. It requires honest setup and separately registered recipients. Each recipient still has keys for its fixed set of questions.

cards.title: A longer encrypted learning run
cards.body: We ran a nonlinear learning rule under TFHE encryption, using an execution schedule generated from Lean. A second process repeated every operation and produced identical encrypted bytes. Decrypting the results also gave the expected states and answers.

cards.title: When repeating a calculation gives different bytes
cards.body: An older encrypted runtime produced different ciphertext bytes on its fourteenth repeated update, despite receiving the same inputs. The replacement runtime uses a fixed plan for its numerical transforms and passes that case and four others. The later 480-operation run uses this approach.

cards.title: Proving the learner’s arithmetic in Lean
cards.body: The proposed Lean package covers learning arithmetic, execution schedules and parts of the cryptographic verifier across 72 modules. Lean checks the mathematical proofs mechanically. The package is available as a patch for the companion proof-system repository; connecting these theorems to the full native implementation remains work to do.

cards.title: How often could a false proof pass?
cards.body: The verifier samples a mathematical encoding instead of checking every step. Its chance of missing an error depends on the number of samples and the error-correcting model. The technical note compares those models and explains why an earlier security estimate was withdrawn.

cards.title: Planning several private steps in advance
cards.body: Functional encryption can let a key reveal a selected result without revealing the input. We use it in a two-step design where each private computation prepares an encrypted state for the next. The steps are set up backwards, so each knows how to encrypt for its successor. This requires the future steps to be planned and the setup secrets erased.

cards.title: An AI whose host cannot open its memory
cards.body: The goal is an AI that can keep learning and communicating while the person running it has no key that opens all of its memory. The remaining keys must allow only the intended operations. This is stronger than storing an encrypted file: the protection has to survive new inputs, new answers and copies of old state.

cards.title: What a post-quantum design would cost
cards.metric_label: per ciphertext in one sizing calculation
cards.body: We studied a lattice-based functional-encryption design intended to resist quantum attacks. One sizing calculation gives about 84 MB per encrypted input and 86 GB of public matrices. Those estimates depend on unresolved construction constants; they show where the storage cost comes from and what needs to shrink before implementation.
